newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aboriginal deaths in custody rising - report.
newsitem.headline: Aboriginal deaths in custody rising - report.

text.p: Aborigines continue to die in prison at a higher rate than other Australians, with indigenous people 1.26 times more likely to die in jail than white prisoners, according an official report released on Monday.
Between May 1989 and May 1996, 96 Aborigines died in either prison or police custody, said the report by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner Mick Dodson.
Despite a A$400 million (US$324 million) government campaign since 1989 to prevent indigenous deaths in custody, 22 Aborigines died in 1995, the highest number in eight years.
In 1996, 16 Aborigines have died in custody.
The main cause of death was suicide by hanging, followed by natural causes as a result of the effects of drugs and alcohol or a lack of proper medical supervision for ill prisoners.

"Why are our people still dying? When are our governments going to feel this pain and anguish...," Dodson said in releasing the report. "Ultimately the blame lies at the foot of the political leaders," he said.
Dodson blamed the death toll on the failure by national, state and territory governments to implement recommendations from a 1989 official inquiry into black deaths in custody.

The 339 royal commission recommendations include the abolition of drunkeness as a criminal offence, imprisonment as a last resort, and upgraded supervision of aboriginal prisoners, especially during their first few hours in custody.

Dodson said that in one case officials did not find one dead aboriginal prisoner until rigor mortis had set in, while another hung himself in a blind spot in his cell's electronic surveillance system.
"Governments may face substantial legal liability if they do not improve their performance," he said, calling for new laws to force reform of the criminal justice system.
The report, titled Indigenous Deaths in Custody 1989 to 1996, said the high death rate reflected the disproportionately high number of Aborigines in custody.
Indigenous people were 17.3 times more likely to be arrested than non-indigenous people, usually for offences such as drunkeness, assault, breaking and entering and car theft.
It also found that across the population as a whole, aboriginal people were 16.5 times more likely to die in custody than non-indigenous people between 1990 and 1995.
While the report found a significant decline in deaths in police custody, two thirds of the deaths now occur in prison.
"The rate of aboriginal deaths in custody has not changed, only the location has changed," Dodson said.
"Many of those who died in custody should not have been in there in the first place," he said.
"Governments agree that imprisonment should be used as a last resort, yet they introduce 'law and order' legislation which restricts the sentencing options open to courts."
One aboriginal woman imprisoned for one month for a minor drug offence hung herself within hours of being jailed.

Lois O'Donoghue, chairwoman of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island Commission, a government sponsored agency that is Australia's peak aboriginal body, said black deaths in custody were the sad results of the dispossession of Australia's indigenous people, the most disadvantaged group in society.

The 300,000 Aborigines in Australia's 18 million population have a life expectancy some 19 years less than the rest of the population. "You have to go back to the history...of colonisation, when our land was removed, our children taken away and families broken up...," O'Donoghue said.
"Until aboriginal people get back their family connections and hold their head up and feel proud as a nation of people we will continue to have these problems," she said.
